name: Aisha Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the rural and community reporter at the Westridge Herald, which is mostly online now, covering the market towns and farms in the hills. I also put together the morning newsletter, and I use AI every day to help sort the overnight emails, draft the event listings and check spellings of place names. Most afternoons I'm out at a livestock market, a village hall or a farm shop. I love the drive and the people; I'm tired of being paid less than the city reporters for twice the miles.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm married to Yusuf, who runs a small catering van that does farmers' markets and weddings. We rent a cottage near the bypass and the van is basically our only asset, and it's not paid off. We've got maybe three weeks of money saved, because everything goes back into the van.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are you finding the job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm still junior and still learning; my editor Helen cuts my stories hard. I'm quick with the tools, and I've set up most of the newsletter process myself. I'm better at the systems than at the writing, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are handy and I'll keep using them, hype or no hype. Online I'd say businesses should use whatever saves time and ignore the noise. At the market I'd just shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a shame, because I was planning to build something with these tools. But my job's fairly steady, because rural news is cheap to keep and nobody else covers it. The van is the real worry, because a wet summer means a thin year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the newsletter with the tools and try to grow its readers, so Helen can sell adverts in it. I'd help Yusuf with an online booking page for the van, built with the same tools. I'd keep trying to put a bit aside each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. Whether AI is hype or not, a wet August at the farmers' markets hurts my family more than any computer could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you and Yusuf in a bad year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We tighten up, and my wage covers the rent while the van pays itself off. Last year we ate a lot of leftover samosas. My parents would help if they had to, but we'd rather not ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the Herald value the newsletter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Helen does. The owners don't really notice it yet. That's why I want the adverts, so it pays for itself and for me.

I'd tell businesses to use whatever **saves time** and ignore the noise.
think: It's a **shame**, because I wanted to build something with these tools.
Rural news is **cheap to keep**, so my job is fairly steady.
do: Grow the **newsletter** so Helen can sell adverts in it.
Build an **online booking page** for Yusuf's catering van.
Keep putting a **little aside** each month.
feel: **Fine**, mostly, with worry about the **van** in a wet year.

fieldNote: Her real exposure is the **catering van**, not AI.

steps.text: Grow the Herald's morning newsletter so it can carry adverts
Build an online booking page for Yusuf's catering van

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance for small outfits like ours, if we're quick. At work I'd offer to bring the tools into the whole newsroom. Online I'd say people should stop waiting for the government and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it's good for me, but not certain. I'm the person who already makes the tools work, so I'd be the last junior to go. I'm still junior, though, and if they cut the rural patch, I'm gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd write a plan for Helen showing how AI could run the listings and the overnight digest, and offer to run it. I'd use the time saved to get out to more farms, because that's what readers can't get anywhere else. And I'd start selling a weekly farm-markets newsletter of my own on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a knot in my stomach about the rural patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd bring the tools into the newsroom. What happens to the people whose jobs that changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of them would have to change what they do. That's work, it changes. I'd try to make sure the listings person, Dot, moves to doing events coverage, because she knows everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you charge for your own newsletter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a small amount. Farmers will pay for a newsletter that tells them lamb prices at Westridge market before the auctioneer has finished his tea.

say: I'd say this is a **chance** for small outfits that move quickly.
I'd tell people to stop **waiting for government** and get on with it.
think: I'd likely be the **last junior** to go, because I make the tools work.
If they **cut the rural patch**, I'm still gone.
do: Write Helen a plan for AI to run the **listings and digest**.
feel: Mostly **hopeful**, with a knot about the **rural patch**.
S1.quote: Farmers will pay for a newsletter that tells them lamb prices at Westridge market before the auctioneer has finished his tea.
fieldNote: She **leads change** at work rather than waiting.

Her **free-market** streak shows in charging farmers for her own newsletter.

steps.text: Write a plan for AI to run the Herald's listings and overnight digest
Visit two extra farms a week with the time saved
Launch a paid weekly farm-markets newsletter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to handle, even people like me who like the tools. I'd say families and communities need to pull together. I'd probably say it at the mosque as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the Herald wouldn't need me by 2028 or 2029. Anything I do at a desk, a computer would do better. My newsletter business goes too, because farmers could ask an AI themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my energy into Yusuf's van, because cooking for people at a wedding is hands-on work and the card says robots take about three years longer. I'd do the marketing and bookings with AI and try to double the events. I'd keep my job as long as they'd pay me and save every penny of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two years means my best skill, getting the tools to work, becomes the thing that makes me unnecessary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the robot gap change things for the van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives the van about three years of being safe, to 2031. People will still want a person making the food at their wedding, maybe even after that. So the van becomes the family business, not the side thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're betting on the van. My dad would worry, because he likes a wage. My mum would ask if she can help with the cooking.

say: I'd say this is **too fast** for anyone, even people who like the tools.
I'd say **families and communities** must pull together.
think: The Herald **wouldn't need me** by 2028 or 2029.
My **newsletter business** goes too, since farmers could ask an AI.
do: Put my energy into **Yusuf's van** and double its events.
Use AI for the van's **marketing and bookings**.
Keep my job and **save every penny** of it.
feel: **Alarmed**, seeing her best skill turn against her.
S2.quote: Two years means my best skill, getting the tools to work, becomes the thing that makes me unnecessary.
fieldNote: Her **tool skills** become the reason she's unneeded.
The **robot gap** turns the catering van into the family business.
She leans on **family** and faith community, not the state.

steps.text: Take over marketing and bookings for Yusuf's catering van
Use AI tools to handle the van's bookings and adverts
Save her full Herald wage until the job ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who start now, so start now. I'd tell younger reporters to learn a skill with their hands too. Online I'd be practical, not gloomy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is decent for me. I'd get three or four years more at the Herald, and I'd use them to build up the van properly. I'd be thirty-two by 2031, which is a fine age to run a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the newsletter going and use the tools at work. On the side, I'd help Yusuf buy a second van in year two, if the bank would lend, so we could do two events at once. I'd start a food hygiene course so I can cook on the van too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it's a busy kind. Five years is enough to turn a catering van into a business, if I stop treating the van as a hobby for Yusuf (her husband).

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A second van is a big risk with three weeks of savings. Why do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because waiting is a bigger risk, in my view. If the job's going anyway, I'd rather own something. We'd only buy it if the bookings for the year were already there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly ourselves, if we didn't plan. Some of it is the big companies rushing, but blaming them doesn't pay the rent.

I'd tell younger reporters to learn a **hands-on skill** too.
think: I'd get **three or four** more years at the Herald.
At **thirty-two**, running a business would be a good fit.
do: Help Yusuf buy a **second van** in year two, if bookings are there.
Take a **food hygiene course** to cook on the van.
Keep the **newsletter** going with the tools at work.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to turn a catering van into a business, if I stop treating the van as a hobby for Yusuf (her husband).
fieldNote: She **takes a risk** on a second van despite thin savings.
She blames **herself first**, a mark of her traditional outlook.
She plans to move from **reporter to business owner** before 2031.

steps.text: Buy a second catering van in year two if bookings are secured

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's use it. I'd say people should learn the tools now and build something of their own. At the mosque I'd say the same to the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is good for me. I'd have time to become a proper reporter, build the newsletter and grow the van. By 2036 I'd want the van to be the main thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at the Herald and grow the paid farm newsletter. We'd pay off the van in two years and buy a second in five. I'd keep learning the tools every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish, with the van always on my mind. With ten years, Yusuf (her husband) and I could build a business our children could one day work in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd like them in a few years. In the slow version, I'd feel all right about it. In the fast one, I'd wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything still bothering you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money is always tight, and the van can have a bad year. But with time, those are normal worries.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** to be used.
I'd tell young people to learn the tools and **build their own** business.
think: Ten years lets me become a **proper reporter** and grow the van.
By **2036** I'd want the van to be the main thing.
do: Grow the **paid farm newsletter** alongside the Herald job.
Pay off the van in two years and buy a **second** in five.
feel: **Calm-ish**, with the **van** always on her mind.
S4.quote: With ten years, Yusuf (her husband) and I could build a business our children could one day work in.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her build a **family business** without rushing.
**Children** depend on the timeline, as with her career plans.

steps.text: Grow the paid farm-markets newsletter to cover its costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My job would go, my newsletter would go, and the van would have to carry us before we're ready. What would help is cheap loans for small family businesses, and less red tape for people starting one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what happens to small towns. If every market town gets its news from the same machine, nobody will notice when the Westridge livestock market quietly shuts.

headlineQuote: If every market town gets its news from the same machine, nobody will notice when the Westridge livestock market quietly shuts.
portrait: Aisha is a **27-year-old** rural reporter at a mostly online regional paper.
She uses **AI every day**, built the newsletter process, and is better at systems than writing.
She's married to Yusuf, who runs a **catering van**, and they have about three weeks saved.
She sees Steady Disruption as **a chance**, but fast AGI makes her best skill a liability.
Her plans turn toward the **van as family business**, using the robot delay for hands-on work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing her job and newsletter before the van can carry them.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for small family businesses and less red tape for starting one.
